extracted.intended_audience: NIH-funded investigators, prospective reviewers, junior faculty (assistant professors), and research faculty interested in NIH peer review service
extracted.subtask_short: serving on NIH peer review panels
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and commentary about the NIH 'expectation' that investigators who receive NIH funding serve on study sections and advisory groups, who is eligible, how to volunteer, and how review service can affect career and funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation for service by NIH-funded PIs
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH 'calls upon investigators who have received research grant funding from the NIH to serve on NIH study sections and advisory groups when invited to do so.' The Notice frames review service as an 'expectation' for funded PIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Notice also states this 'expectation for service is entirely voluntary and an inability to serve has no impact on an investigator’s ability to compete for grant support' — i.e., the language is intentionally weak/contradictory. The author urges readers to treat review service as a default professional expectation despite the voluntary wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is eligible / may volunteer to serve
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals who possess expertise in areas supported by the NIH and who wish to volunteer to serve in the NIH peer review process should self-identify; NSF-funded PIs and others with relevant expertise can be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To volunteer, send an email to the Enhancing Peer Review mailbox (EnhancingPeerReview@mail.nih.gov) with a brief description of areas of expertise and a copy of your biosketch. The post explicitly encourages even raw assistant professors and those on the job market to volunteer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical selection preference: funded PIs preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Most Scientific Review Officers (SROs) and selection practices commonly prefer reviewers who are funded/are PIs; many SROs 'won’t bring someone in if they are not funded.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not an absolute rule — exceptions occur for individuals with superlative expertise, corporate scientists, or other special cases — but being funded is a commonly applied standard that increases the chance of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-PI and special-case reviewer exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although being a PI is commonly expected, non-PIs have served on panels (e.g., Special Emphasis Panels) if they have the right expertise or circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include non-PI reviewers on Special Emphasis Panels or corporate/industry scientists brought in by SROs; these are exceptions rather than the norm and may provoke resistance from some reviewers or chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program staff can consider review service in funding 'gray zone' decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH program officers have latitude to fund grants as 'exceptions' to the priority score/percentile in the gray funding zone and can factor in program interests and human-interaction factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contends that program officers can and do consider review service and 'team playing' when making pickups in the gray zone. He suggests PIs may reasonably assume that prior review service could be a positive factor in these discretionary funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: POs should ask/review prior reviewer service as part of funding discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: Program Officers (line POs) can and should ask PIs who call them whether the PI has served on a study section, the type of service (ad hoc or appointed), and how recent it was.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subtlety fails, POs can 'parrot' the Notice about the new expectation. The author also suggests adding a line to the 'Other Support' page submitted prior to funding that records review service to make the information prominent during funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serving on study section is valuable professional training (grantsmanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Serving on review panels teaches grantsmanship: reviewing your stack and seeing others' reviews provides concrete lessons for improving your own proposals and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal evidence in the post: one author/reviewer states that reviewing contributed to securing a subsequent R01. The post recommends even junior faculty participate via ad hoc service, Special Emphasis Panels, or small business review opportunities to gain experience without full-term workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh service workload against career stage and research demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Department chairs often advise junior faculty to avoid full-fledged study section service early in their careers because it can take time away from research necessary for tenure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider nuances: ad hoc reviewing or limited commitments (SEPs, small-business reviews) may be appropriate earlier; decisions should depend on current funding status, lab staffing, and the individual's ability to handle additional workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical recommendation: cultivate relationships with Program staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Building personal relationships with NIH program staff can influence discretionary funding decisions in the gray zone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author suggests trainees visit program staff at meeting booths and otherwise develop rapport; this is presented as real-world human-interaction factor that PIs often believe affects pickups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/practical gap between the Notice and peer-review reality
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a disconnect between the NIH's formal 'expectation' and actual recruiting/practice; longstanding criticisms exist about peer-review quality and recruitment difficulties amid more proposals and less funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are warned that notices alone don't instantly change institutional culture; systemic issues (more applicants chasing less money, inconsistent reviews) persist and impact how review service is perceived and how panels are staffed.
